compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
The three shared letters explain where the descriptions overlap. Both describe preferences for noticing possibilities, weighing people and values, and keeping outward options open. A particular person may express those preferences in many ways.

The two fictional coordinators below both care about how volunteers receive the invitation. Either can make a direct request, stay quiet in a meeting or suggest another way to help.

The four-letter difference is E/I. Someone with an Extraversion preference may find it easier to develop a thought through interaction. Someone with an Introversion preference may find it easier to work through it privately. Both can find either setting useful.

Both coordinators have the same draft, contact list, deadline and say in the wording. Either might work through the message by talking with a teammate or by thinking through the same draft alone.

compare_blocks.body:
Boundary of use: the recruitment, the rota and the friends' group chat below are editorial fiction, used only to practise discrimination, corresponding to no real event or person. Recruitment data evaluates the activity and does not enter any division of work or assessment; who takes which segment follows skill, willingness, available time and what the project needs, not type.

On a volunteer project, people can disagree about how much time to spend refining an invitation. Agree when the wording needs to be ready and who will make the final decision. That keeps the conversation on the task.

### ENFP and INFP: recruitment — both ways of writing can work

(Fictional scene) In the same team, recruitment can be made into a lively occasion: ask the talkative people in the group to forward it, describe sorting old books as coming to leaf through what others donated, promise food. Or it can be made into something that does not press anyone: state exactly what the two hours involve, that coming once is fine, that no uniform is needed. Both are available options; either type may choose one, or write both.

The risk of the first is a crowd that disperses quickly; the risk of the second is that it looks so gentle nobody takes it seriously. An effective combination separates the tone from the reach: whoever writes nuance better writes the copy, whoever is in more groups handles the channels, and neither rewrites the other's draft — the division follows ability and time, not type.

To compare the two versions, a small test is possible, but its purpose is choosing copy, not verifying type: write two versions, one listing tasks and slots, one explaining why this is worth coming to, keeping channel, send time and task information as similar as possible, and send each to half the list; record reach, sign-ups and attendance separately, and after the event ask those who did not come why. Many questions and few arrivals may mean the commitment exceeded what was actually arranged, or the slot, the group or a last-minute change — all these explanations have to be kept open, and one set of numbers cannot settle it.

### ENFP and INFP: the rota — nobody wants the sign-out desk

(Fictional scene) While building the rota, the sign-out desk sits unclaimed for two and a half hours, and both volunteers say they are not good with strangers. Do not guess the reason for them; ask what specifically is hard: shyness, needing to collect a child, or two and a half hours on their feet. Ask first, then discuss options.

One option redesigns the job: turn the desk into a welcome point with bookmarks to hand out, half an hour each, with the task written more concretely. The other changes the conditions: pair them with someone experienced, move the table somewhere less conspicuous, allow no name badge. The first may only have changed the label while the resistance remains; the second may make the lending records messier. Both can be done at once, or one tried for a week.

If the rota cannot be filled for two weeks running, the problem is probably not preference but hands and rules. What needs discussing is adding people, shortening the shift, moving to a rotation, or dropping one service — not who is more considerate.

### ENFP and INFP: someone keeps posting ads in the friends' group

In this fictional group chat, a member posts shop links three times a week and the others gradually stop talking. Anyone in the group might suggest a dedicated thread or ask how a new rule would affect the person posting. These questions concern possible responses and their effect on people. They cannot distinguish ENFP from INFP.

A separate thread might make room for conversation or add a rule nobody uses. Talking to the person directly might settle the issue or reveal a concern the others had missed. The group’s response depends on the people and their agreement.

If you want to raise the issue, name what has changed, ask what the group wants and explain the proposal to the member. The fictional example illustrates how to handle a shared problem without assigning motives by type.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread takes E for having many friends and I for not fitting in. An ENFP has weeks of not wanting to reply to anything, and an INFP can talk until midnight in a circle they know. Neither the number of social contacts nor reply speed is a reading of the first letter.

Hesitation and fluent speech can have many causes. Someone may wait to find the right words or think aloud as they form a view. How they speak tells you little about how much they care.

The third uses send speed and revision count as a ruler. Someone sending immediately may simply have no time to revise that day; someone on a fifth version may simply care unusually much about this event. Speed depends on time, role and fluency, and is not an E/I indicator — looking more often does not change that.

The fourth writes it as who is better suited to lead. Getting people to come, writing steady copy and filling a rota are all trainable; missing any one of them and the team will not survive a third event. A real division looks at who can do it, who has time and who is willing.

### ENFP and INFP: recruitment — both ways of writing can work

(Fictional scene) In the same team, recruitment can be made into a lively occasion: ask the talkative people in the group to forward it, describe sorting old books as coming to leaf through what others donated, promise food. Or it can be made into something that does not press anyone: state exactly what the two hours involve, that coming once is fine, that no uniform is needed. Both are available options; either type may choose one, or write both.

The risk of the first is a crowd that disperses quickly; the risk of the second is that it looks so gentle nobody takes it seriously. An effective combination separates the tone from the reach: whoever writes nuance better writes the copy, whoever is in more groups handles the channels, and neither rewrites the other's draft — the division follows ability and time, not type.

One option redesigns the job: turn the desk into a welcome point with bookmarks to hand out, half an hour each, with the task written more concretely. The other changes the conditions: pair them with someone experienced, move the table somewhere less conspicuous, allow no name badge. List what the project needs, such as writing the invitation, organising the shift schedule or answering questions. Ask who has the time, experience and interest to do each part.
items.question: Which is better suited to leading a volunteer project?

items.answer:
A team can get stuck if one person thinks the plan is still open while another has begun sharing it with volunteers. Check which decisions are settled and which can change.

A workable agreement uses two lists: what must be settled this week (venue, slot, headcount ceiling) and what can be adjusted as work proceeds (wording, division detail, whether to add a segment). External commitments are voiced by the person handling contact, and changes get a heads-up. Lists are more useful than guessing at someone's character.
items.question: Where do they most often jam?

items.answer:
Different answering situations may affect which experiences come to mind. If the same assessment provides comparable dimension scores and E/I is close to its threshold, a small score difference can also change the first letter.

With only a type and no dimension scores or scoring notes, do not infer whether it is near a boundary. What can be done is to check the assessment's name, version and language, review whether you were referring to your own habit or to the role at the time, and retest in a similar situation; different results again are normal, and there is no need to force a choice.

Framework sources: preference definitions follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

Four-position convention on this page: Ne–Fi–Te–Si for ENFP and Fi–Ne–Si–Te for INFP follow the common four-function notation adopted here; in particular the attitude of the third process is labelled inconsistently across sources, and this page does not present the writing as the Foundation's only reading, nor use position to infer behaviour order, areas of strength, collaboration or attraction.

Editorial fiction note: the recruitment, the rota and the friends' group chat, and the two characters in them, are editorial fiction used only to practise discrimination, corresponding to no real activity, organisation or person, and constituting no assessment of anyone.

Scope limits: this page discusses emphasis between preferences, not a ranking of ability, and is not for hiring screens or predicting relationships; clinical judgement belongs to qualified professionals. The activity measures mentioned can only evaluate the activity itself and cannot verify a type.
